A subsequent review4 that included this later study concluded that there was benefit with the use of adjuvant fluorouracil, but that chemoradiotherapy should not yet be dismissed from further study because tri- als to date had used radiotherapy regimens that were now considered to be suboptimal, a view also adopted by US guidelines.5 Adjuvant gemcitabine is also effective,6 and some consider it the preferred drug if single-agent therapy is used.5,7 It is also recommended for use with fluorour- acil-based chemoradiation. Capecitabine is an alternative to gemcitabine or fluorouracil for monotherapy.5 Pre-oper- ative (neoadjuvant) chemoradiotherapy is also under in- vestigation, but a survival benefit has not been proven, and toxicity can be severe.1,8,9 In patients with symptomatic localised unresectable dis- ease, chemoradiotherapy may be used.5 Most studies have reported a modest survival benefit from the combination of radiotherapy and fluorouracil.1,5,9,10 Evidence suggests that radiotherapy with gemcitabine can yield similar out- comes.5 A period of chemotherapy followed by chemora- diation may be preferable to first-line chemoradiation. Chemotherapy alone is also an option in these patients,5 and a systematic review11 found insufficient evidence to recommend chemoradiation over chemotherapy alone; gemcitabine monotherapy or gemcitabine-based combina- tion therapy is advocated.5 Use of neoadjuvant chemoradi- otherapy to improve resectability rates in locally advanced disease is investigational.5,8,10 In patients with advanced (metastatic) disease, supportive care alone remains appro- priate for those with poor performance status. Palliative chemotherapy may be considered in those with adequate performance status,5 but benefits are modest (pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a chemoresistant tumour).1,12 Despite this, a meta-analysis13 found a survival advantage for chemotherapy over best supportive care. Single-agent fluorouracil has been widely used.6,8,14 Combination regi- mens, such as FAM (fluorouracil, doxorubicin, mitomy- cin) SMF (streptozocin, mitomycin, fluorouracil), and FAP (fluorouracil, doxorubicin, cisplatin), have not proved more effective than fluorouracil alone.8,9 However, there is evidence5,15 that gemcitabine can produce slightly better survival than fluorouracil in patients who can toler- ate it, and it has been recommended as the standard of care.1,5,8,9,16 There is also some evidence that its effective- ness may be improved if it is given at a fixed dose rate of 10 mg/m2 per minute, rather than by conventional infu- sion.5,14 Gemcitabine has also been investigated in combi- nation with other drugs such as ci
